draft.briefing: Hey, you're in Morjim! This stretch on the north bank of the Chapora River estuary is a nesting site for olive ridley sea turtles. So many Russians have settled here that people call it 'Little Russia'.
draft.hungryLine: The beach restaurants here do pizzas, Goan and North Indian food, and a few Russian joints even serve borscht by the sea.

moodReplies.show-me-around: Walk 9 minutes to Milagres Church, then carry on to Santa Cruz Chapel and the Morje Kuladevta temple.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: The beach here is quiet and untraveled compared to Goa's resort strips, and in season the water is pleasant for wading.
moodReplies.surprise-me: Morjim is pronounced 'Morji', the second m is silent.

tips.title: Swim while lifeguards are on.
tips.body: Lifeguards are on duty from sunrise to sunset, so stick to those hours for a dip.

tips.title: Give kitesurfing a go.
tips.body: The shallow sea and very wide beach make it a kitesurfing favourite, and rentals are available right on the beach.

story.title: Birds and turtles
story.body: Morjim sits on the northern bank of the Chapora River estuary. It has long been home to a variety of birds and to nesting olive ridley turtles.

story.title: Little Russia
story.body: A boom in Russian visitors and settlers earned the village the nickname 'Little Russia'. Some local politicians have objected to the Russian presence.

story.title: A census town
story.body: The 2011 census counted 6,760 people in Morjim. Literacy here was higher than the Goa state average.

story.title: Kites over the sand
story.body: Far from Goa's main resorts, the beach stays relatively quiet. Kitesurfers love its shallow water and wide sands.
